title: Software Supply-Chain Provenance
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of software supply-chain provenance and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to software supply-chain provenance.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on software supply-chain provenance. Provenance records how an artifact was built and which source revision produced it; verification helps detect mismatched or untrusted published artifacts. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Software Supply-Chain Provenance matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Provenance records how an artifact was built and which source revision produced it; verification helps detect mismatched or untrusted published artifacts. Publishing is a supply-chain boundary. Make versions traceable to source commits, authenticate with scoped credentials, record provenance where supported, and validate artifacts before promotion.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Provenance records how an artifact was built and which source revision produced it; verification helps detect mismatched or untrusted published artifacts. Publishing is a supply-chain boundary. Make versions traceable to source commits, authenticate with scoped credentials, record provenance where supported, and validate artifacts before promotion. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

content_blocks.code:
name: Build with provenance
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write
  attestations: write
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: mkdir -p dist && echo "demo" > dist/output.txt
      - uses: actions/attest-build-provenance@v2
        with:
          subject-path: dist/output.txt
content_blocks.expected_output: The example requests an attestation for the specified file; an actual production workflow should use reviewed, pinned actions and verify the resulting attestation.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run only in a disposable repository that supports artifact attestations and verify the provider’s current prerequisites.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove attestation permission if the workflow does not generate attestations.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to software supply-chain provenance. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain software supply-chain provenance, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Publish packages and container images with traceable versions and integrity checks.

content.task: Apply software supply-chain provenance to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Provenance records how an artifact was built and which source revision produced it; verification helps detect mismatched or untrusted published artifacts.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Provenance records how an artifact was built and which source revision produced it; verification helps detect mismatched or untrusted published artifacts. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.

Publishing is a supply-chain boundary. Make versions traceable to source commits, authenticate with scoped credentials, record provenance where supported, and validate artifacts before promotion.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
